headline: Ascend Wellness agrees $35.5M deal for 5 Ohio stores and a grow
dek: Ascend's 8-K of 20 November shows it and a financed partner buying Greenleaf's Ohio grow and five stores, with 36% paid after closing.
key_points: Ascend Wellness disclosed on 20 November that its Ohio subsidiary and a financed partner agreed to buy five dispensaries and a cultivation facility from the Greenleaf group for $35.5 million in cash.
Ascend's own subsidiary takes the grow and one store in Akron; a third-party Retail Buyer that Ascend finances and supports takes the other four dispensaries.
By MetaFlora's arithmetic, $12.7 million, or 36% of the price, falls due 12 and 18 months after closing; only $3.55 million is paid up front.
Closing needs all required regulatory approvals, and the filing gives no expected date; The Marijuana Herald says Ascend's Ohio footprint would reach 12 stores including affiliates.
body: Ascend Wellness Holdings has agreed to buy its way deeper into Ohio. In a Form 8-K filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Friday 20 November, the New Jersey-based operator said its Ohio subsidiary and a partner company signed an agreement to acquire a cultivation facility and five dispensaries from the Greenleaf group for $35.5 million in cash.

The deal splits the assets in two. Ohio Patient Access, LLC, a wholly owned Ascend subsidiary, takes the cultivation facility and one dispensary in Akron. A separate company the filing calls the Retail Buyer, a third party to which Ascend provides financing and support services, takes the other four stores. The sellers are Greenleaf Apothecaries, Greenleaf Gardens, Greenleaf Therapeutics and High Street Capital Partners. Closing depends on regulatory approval, and Ascend has not given a date.

The filing is short. It names only one location, Akron, and does not give the address of the cultivation facility or the towns of the other four dispensaries. It says the agreement carries the usual representations, warranties and covenants, adjustments for inventory and cash, and indemnification subject to limits. No press release was attached; the only exhibit is the cover-page data file.

The Marijuana Herald, which reported the filing on 21 November, says the purchase would take Ascend's Ohio retail footprint to 12 dispensaries, counting affiliated locations. As we reported on 13 November, Ascend had just opened its seventh Ohio store, in Lewis Center, and ended its expansion run with 61 stores across its markets including partner-owned locations, beating a year-end goal of 60. Adding five Ohio stores would push that count well past the target before the year is out, if approvals arrive in time, which the filing does not suggest.

The cultivation facility matters as much as the shops. Owning supply in a state lets a retailer control product mix and margins rather than buying wholesale from competitors. Ascend's own website describes its footprint as concentrated in limited-licence, adult-use and near-adult-use markets in the Northeast and Midwest, and Ohio fits that pattern.

The payment schedule is the most telling part of the filing. Ascend and the Retail Buyer pay a $3,550,000 deposit up front. A further $4,072,500 is due when management services agreements take effect; those agreements, which let the buyers run the assets before the deal closes, also need regulatory approval. Another $15,150,000 is paid at closing.

The remainder is deferred: $6,226,250 on the first anniversary of closing and $6,501,250 eighteen months after closing. By MetaFlora's arithmetic, that deferred portion totals $12,727,500, about 36% of the price. The up-front deposit is 10%, and the cash at closing is about 43%. The filing describes all of it as cash consideration; it mentions no shares or seller notes.
> A third of the price is paid after closing, so Ascend is partly buying the Ohio stores with the cash they are expected to generate.

Splitting the deal between an owned subsidiary and a financed partner is a familiar way for multistate operators to grow in states that limit how many licences one company may hold. The filing does not say why Ascend chose this structure for Ohio, and none of the sources we read states an Ohio per-company cap, so we do not attribute the split to one. What the filing does make clear is that Ascend's economic tie to the four partner stores runs through financing and services, not ownership.

Ohio's market gives context for the price. Adult-use sales began on 6 August 2024 at existing medical dispensaries, and Senate Bill 56 caps the number of dispensaries at 400 statewide, according to our Ohio legal hub. A fixed ceiling on stores tends to make existing licences scarcer and more valuable, which is one reason operators buy rather than build.

The deal follows a third quarter in which Ascend reported net revenue of $130.0 million, up 4.2% from a year earlier, and adjusted EBITDA of $31.1 million, as we reported on 13 November. The company has also said a reverse split approved in August could support a listing on a major US exchange. A cash acquisition of this size, with a large deferred tail, keeps more money on the balance sheet in the near term while that plan plays out.

Ascend is also working through a separate purchase in Massachusetts, where it runs two Worcester and Shrewsbury dispensaries under a consulting agreement while it waits for approval to close. The Ohio deal has the same shape: operate first under a services agreement, close later once regulators sign off.

Ascend has interests beyond Ohio in the federal fight now playing out in court. A Pennsylvania company that Kind Green Buds describes as affiliated with Ascend is among the four that joined the D.C. Circuit challenge to the DEA's 29 November supply-chain deadline, as we reported on 21 November. That case concerns medical licences only: the rescheduling order leaves adult-use cannabis in Schedule I, as Maryland's regulator restated on 20 November.

The first signal is regulatory: whether Ohio's Division of Cannabis Control approves the management services agreements, which would trigger the second payment and put Ascend's team in charge of the stores before closing. The second is whether Ascend names the four partner dispensaries and the cultivation site in a press release or its next quarterly filing. The third is timing. The filing sets no outside date, so the 12- and 18-month payments could land anywhere from late 2027 onward, depending on when the deal closes.
